title: Rama gives it all away
hook: before he leaves, Rama gives everything away, and makes a poor old man throw his stick
carry: dana: give generously, and give humbly

segments.voice: Yesterday: Urmila, left in Valmiki's silence, and seva, Lakshmana's anger turned into service. Today the departure begins, with giving.

Armlets. Earrings. A golden girdle. A herd of cows. On the day Rama leaves, his rooms empty out, piece by piece, into other people's hands. Leaving a home can come with a day like this, sad and oddly freeing at once: the couch to a cousin, the plants to whoever will water them. Here it's a prince's wealth. And in the middle of it, Valmiki tells a small story with a joke in it, on a day built for tears.
screen: `ARMLETS, EARRINGS, COWS.` → `A PRINCE'S WEALTH, GIVEN AWAY.` → `A JOKE ON A DAY OF TEARS.`

segments.voice: Rama sends for Suyajna, the son of his teacher Vasishtha, and gives him armlets, earrings and jewels. Sita sends a necklace and a golden girdle to Suyajna's wife. Gifts go to teachers, to old household servants, to everyone who depends on Rama for a living, so no one is left without support while he's gone. Then the story. Near Ayodhya lives a very poor brahmin named Trijata, old and thin, who scrapes a living digging in the fields. His wife hears Rama is giving things away. Go, she says. So Trijata stands before the prince, and Rama, of all things, teases him. I haven't yet given away even a thousand of my cows. Throw your staff. However far it lands, every cow up to that point is yours. The old man ties up his clothes and throws with every bit of strength he has. The staff flies across the river Sarayu into a pasture full of cattle. Rama embraces him and gives him every cow up to that spot. Then he apologizes. Don't be offended. It was a joke. I only wanted to see the strength in you. This is dana, giving, one of the oldest duties in Hinduism, and Hindus still give it at turning points: weddings, festivals, journeys. An Upanishad teacher sends his students home with a short list on how: give with faith, give with modesty, give with understanding. Rama gives a fortune, then says sorry to the poorest man in line. That's the modest part, and the hardest. Grief hasn't made him small, and wealth hasn't made him proud.
screen: `GIFTS SO NO ONE IS LEFT WITHOUT.` · `THROW YOUR STAFF.` · `IT WAS A JOKE. FORGIVE ME.` · `DANA: WITH FAITH, WITH MODESTY.` · then, large: `GRIEF HASN'T MADE HIM SMALL.`

segments.voice: Look around in your mind at what you own, and pick one thing someone else would use. Picture handing it over the way the Upanishad asks: with faith, with modesty, without needing thanks. If you pray, offer it to God first; if you don't, simply wish the receiver well. Then rest in the breath, lighter by one thing.
The departure, part one: giving. Rama and Sita give their wealth away, and Rama gives poor Trijata every cow up to where his staff lands, then says sorry for the joke.
Hold on to it: dana, give generously, and give humbly. That's day five hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Hindus give dana, gifts, at turning points such as weddings, festivals and journeys; the Taittiriya Upanishad asks that it be given with faith and with modesty, and Rama's apology to Trijata shows the modest part.
